chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Zurara, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the testimony of the people of the (other) religions. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'Not allowed, except against the people of their own religions. So if others cannot be found, their testimony would be allowed upon the bequest, because it is not correct for a right of anyone to go away'.
ai.seo_question: When is the testimony of non-Muslims accepted in Shia Islamic law?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi outlines the principle of 'la yuslih dhahab huqq ahad' (preventing the loss of anyone's right) to justify accepting non-Muslim testimony in bequests when no Muslim witnesses are available. It reflects the Shia juristic view that while religious affiliation generally restricts legal competence, the preservation of property rights takes precedence in the absence of alternatives. This ruling underscores the pragmatic flexibility within Shia fiqh regarding inter-communal legal interactions.
